 93. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be 
pleased to state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that forty-nine infant s died at AIIMS while being subjected to clinical 
trials for testing new drugs and therapies over the last two and a half years; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof; 
 (c) whether foreign manufactured medicines were listed during the trials; 
 (d)  if so, the details thereof; 
 (e) how many children were admi tted for these clinical trials and how many sets of trials 
were conducted on these children; 
 (f) whether the parents of these children were well informed about these clinical trials and 
were given social counseling before these trials; and 
 (g) if so, the details thereof? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST R Y  O F   H E A L T H  A N D  F A M I L Y  W E L F A R E  
(SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) Death of  49 children enrolled in 6 clinical trials 
at All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi was reported between January 2006 and 
June, 2008. These consisted of 4 clinical trials with drugs as interventions, one trial with feeding 
protocol and one with Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP). It was observed that 4142 
children were enrolled in 42 clinical trials in the Department of Paediatrics. 
 (c) and (d) Yes, Sir. In one case, the fore ign manufactured medicines were used during 
the trials. Zinc deficiency is of public health  importance in India because of the problem of 
widespread zinc deficiency. WHO/UNICEF, Indian Academy of Pediatrics and the National Rural 
Health Mission, Govt. of India recommend use of zinc in treatment of acute diarrhea in all infants 
and children. This policy is based on large well  done randomized controlled studies from many 

 147 
 
developing countries, and different parts of India including AIIMS. Zinc is important in human 
biology and its deficiency impairs various immune and non immune defence against infections. 
Low levels of zinc in the cord blood and in infants, particularly so in the low birth weight, who 
constitute one-third of all births in India and co ntribute maximally to the increased infant deaths. 
Neonatal sepsis is an important cause of death in  these infants. The intent of the study was to 
provide a cheap, safe and efficacious treatment in  addition to antibiotics for serious bacterial 
infection in neonates and young infants. The Government of India has been encouraging the 
public sector companies and the drug industry to prepare cheap dispersible zinc tablets. The 
Lancet has rated use of zinc in sick children in diarrhea as one of the 10 essential interventions 
for all child health programmes in the developing world. 
 (e) 1073 children were admitted for these clinical trials and 42 clinical trials were conducted 
on these children. 
 (f) and (g) Yes, Sir. The parents of these children were counselled before these trials and 
written consent were obtained from the parents/guardians of the children.

 118.  SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
   DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY:  
 Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state:

fund from the passengers even after its expiry on 31st March, 2007;

 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI R. VELU): (a) and (c) 
Yes, Sir. 
 (b) The Committee noted that the Railways have subsumed the safety surcharge in the 
passenger tariff for part funding of the Dedicated Freight Corridor and other infrastructure 
projects and expressed their disapproval of the same. They strongly recommended that this 
practice should not be adopted by the Railways and that the Ministry should review the decision 
taken to replace the safety surcharge with development charge. 
 (d) The main reason for subsuming the safety surcharge in the passenger tariff is the 
fact that despite increase in input costs and wholesale price index, there has been no increase 
in passenger fares since 2002-03. On the contrary, passenger fares have been reduced in the 
last few successive Railway Budgets. The mass ive expansion required in rail infrastructure 
both for meeting passenger and freight needs, in synchronization with the requirement of the 
growing economy, has placed considerable burden on the Railways are also not getting 
adequate gross budgetary support and are increasingly relying on internal generation and 
market borrowing for financing crucial infrastr ucture. As market borrowing becomes more and 
more expensive, it would be difficult for the Railways to consider withdrawal of the 
Development Charge.

Increase in price of iron ore 
 155. SHRI DHARAM PAL SABHARWAL: Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to  
state: 

 189
 (a) whether it is a fact that Government is considering various measures to check and 
contain the prices of iron ore including ban on export of iron ore; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof; 
 (c) whether Government is aware that steel manufacturers are facing a lot of hardships 
due to increase in prices of iron ore; and 
 (d) if so, the steps being taken to  contain the prices of iron ore? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI JITIN PRASADA): (a) and 
(b) With a view to make available iron ore to domestic iron and steel industry at an affordable 
price, Government of India has imposed an ad-valorem export duty of 15% on all varieties of 
iron ore w.e.f. 13th June, 2008. However, ban on export of iron ore is presently not under 
consideration of the Government. 
 (c) and (d) It has been brought to notice by sponge iron producers and pig iron 
producers, who procure iron ore mainly on spot basis, that they are facing problems in getting 
iron ore supply at affordable prices, thereby affecting their economic viability. However, recently, 
the spot prices of iron ore in  the global market have witne ssed a declining trend. This is 
expected to result in decrease in the domestic prices of iron ore also.

DISQUALIFICATION OF A MEMBER ON GROUND OF DEFECTION 
 MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon’ble Members, I have to make the following announcement: 
 Shri Veer Singh, Member, Rajya Sabha, filed before the then Chairman, Rajya Sabha, 
Shri Bhairon Singh Shekhawat, a petition da ted 4th April 2007, under paragraph 6 of the 
Tenth Schedule to the Constitution and Rule 6 of the Members of Rajya Sabha 
(Disqualification on grounds of Defection) Rules, 1985, praying that the Chairman, Rajya 
Sabha, be pleased to hold that Shri Isam Singh, Member, Rajya Sabha, stands 
disqualified under the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution of India and also declare his 
seat in the Rajya Sabha vacant. The then Chairman forwarded copies of the petition and 
the annexures thereto to Shri lsam Singh and Sushri Mayawati, the then Leader of the 
Bahujan Samaj Party in Rajya Sabha, under rule 7(3) of the said Rules, on the 20th of 
April, 2007, requesting them to forward their comments on the petition to him within 
seven days from the receipt of the same. 
 Sushri Mayawati in her comments agreed with the contention of the petitioner and 
contended that Shri ls am Singh, who had been  elected to the Rajya Sabha from the State of 
Uttar Pradesh as a candidate of the Bahujan Samaj Party , was expelled from the party for 
violating the party norms and for anti-party activities. Further, his act of forming a new political 

 195
party “Bahujan Kranti Party ” on the 10th September, 2006 and his becoming its National 
President is a conduct that indicates that he has voluntarily given up the membership of the 
Bahujan Samaj Party and, therefore, be disqualified w.e.f. 10th September, 2006. 
 Shri Isam Singh in his comments disagreed wi th the charges made against him. Shri Isam 
Singh contested the contents of the petition. He denied having received any Show Cause Notice 
and said that it was a manipulated document meant for his harassment. In fact, he came to 
know about his suspension from the Party from media. He denied making false allegations 
against Sushri Mayawati and accused her of taking a dictatorial action, when he tried to uplift the 
image of the Party. Shri Isam Singh denied the charges of voluntarily giving up membership of 
the Bahujan Samaj Party and joining a new political party. He also stated that he had formed a 
new political party only after his expulsion from the BSP, and hence there was no question of his 
disqualification as a Member of Rajya Sabha. He requested that Shri Veer Singh’s petition 
seeking his disqualification may be dismissed. 
 After considering the comments of Sushri Mayawa ti as well as of Shri Isam Singh in relation 
to the petition, the then Chairman was satisfied, having regard to the nature and circumstances 
of the case that it was necessary to refer the petition to the Committee of Privileges of the Rajya 
Sabha for making a preliminary inquiry and submitting a report to him, under sub-rule (4) of 
Rule 7 of the Rules and ordered accordingly on 24th July, 2007. 
 The Committee of Privileges submitted it s Report to me on the 22nd May, 2008. 
 On receipt of this Report, I forwarded a copy thereof to Shri Isam Singh and gave him 
opportunities to appear before me on July I and 4, 2008 to represent his case and to be heard in 
person in terms of Rule 7 (7) of the Members of Rajya Sabha (Disqualification on ground of 
Defection) Rules, 1985. 
 Taking into account the facts of the case and the report of the Committee of Privileges and 
in accordance with the provisions of article 102 (2) read with the Tenth Schedule to the 
Constitution of India, I decided and declared by an order as follows: 
 “In exercise of the powers conferred upon me under article 102(2) read with paragraph 6 of 
the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution of India, I, Mohammad Hamid Ansari, Chairman, 
Rajya Sabha, hereby decide th at Shri lsam Singh, an elec ted member of the Rajya Sabha 
from the State of Uttar Pradesh, by voluntarily giving up his membership of the Bahujan 
Samaj Party, his original political party, has become subject to disqualification for being a 
Member of the Rajya Sabha in terms of paragraph 2(1)(a) of the Tenth Schedule to the 
Constitution of India.” Accordingly, Shri Isham Singh has ceased to be a Member of Rajya 
Sabha with effect from 4th July, 2008.

MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the passing

Shri Sharma was born in September, 1933 at village Karondia, District Bhopal of
Madhya Pradesh, and had his education at Vikram University, Ujjain.
An agriculturist by vocation, Shri Sharma began his career as a teacher and was
associated with various social welfare organisations. Shri Sharma started his legislative
career with the Membership of the Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly in 1967 and
was a Member of that Assembly continuously for 35 years. He also served as Minister
of Co-operatives, Revenue and Agriculture in the Government of Madhya Pradesh.
Shri Sharma represented the State of Madhya Pradesh in this House from June,
2004, till his sad demise.

Parliamentarian, an administrator and a noted social worker. We deeply mourn the
passing away of Shri Laxminarayan Sharma.

WRITTEN ANSWERS TO STARRED QUESTIONS 
Small Savings Schemes 
 †*41. SHRI MANOHAR JOSHI : Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that the depo sits in small savings schemes being run  
through post offices have reduced due to reduction in interest rates during the last few years;  
 (b) whether it is also a fact that intere st rates being offered by banks are higher;  
 (c) if so, whether Government as considering to make the interest rate of small savings 
schemes equal to those of the banks; 
 (d) if so, the details thereof; and  
 (e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
 THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) Interest rates on Small 
savings Schemes have remained unchanged since 1st March, 2003. The gross small savings 
collections during 2006-07 at Rs. 1,82,181 crore declined to Rs. 1,40,443 crore during 2007-08 
(Provisional). The decline of 23 per cent in gross collections under various small savings 
schemes reflects, inter-alia, investors’ preference for alternative savings instruments. 
 (b) Yes, Sir.  
 (c) and (d) There is no proposal under consid eration of Government to make the interest 
rate of Small Savings Schemes equal to those of the banks.  
 (e) Interest rates on small savings schemes ar e Administered Interest Rates. High rates of 
administered interest have fiscal implications an d therefore, need to be linked to the cost of 
borrowings by the Central Government. As pe r the recommendations of the Committee on 
Administered Interest Rates and Other Related Issues Chaired by Dr. Y.V. Reddy, the then 
Deputy Governor, RBI, these interest rates are benchmarked to the average yield on 
Government Securities  (G-Sec.) of comparab le maturity in the secondary market, with a 
suitable spread up to 50 basis points depending upon the maturity and liquidity of the 
instruments. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

 4 
 Recent analysis shows that while the average yield on Government S ecurities of shorter 
maturities (one to three years) is at present slig htly higher compared to interest rates on Small 
Savings Schemes of comparable ma turities, the interest rates on  Post Office Monthly Income 
Account (POMIA), NSC-VIII Issue, Kisan Vikas Patra and Senior Citizens Saving Scheme still 
enjoy a reasonable spread over G-Sec. yield. 
 Net collections under small savings schemes are on lent to the States and serve as a source 
of funding their Annual Plans. Any increase in the small savings interest  rates will result in a 
concomitant increase in the on-lending rate to  the States. The State Governments have not 
been comfortable even with the existing rates of 9.5% for 25 years and any increase thereof will 
imply higher debt servicing costs and is likely to be resisted.  
CNG filling stations in NCR 
 *42. SHRI HARISH RAWAT:  
   SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
 Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL) has failed to provide adequate number of 
CNG filling stations in the National Capital an d NCR town resulting in inconvenience to CNG 
vehicle owners; 
 (b) if so, the reasons therefor;  
 (c) whether CNG vehicle owners have to wait hours together to get fuel from the CNG 
stations; and  
 (d) if so, the steps taken by Government to set up more CNG stations in the National 
Capital and NCR towns and also to increase the filling capacity of the existing CNG stations? 
 THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MURLI DEORA): (a) and (b) 
At present, IGL has 163 CNG stations in Delhi, the highest number in any city in India. There are 
469 dispensers installed in thes e stations, catering to around 2,50,000 vehicles. Non-availability 
of land has been a constraint in setting up CNG stations. The  number of CNG run private cars in 
Delhi has increased phenomenally in the past few months because of the differential in prices of 
petrol / diesel and CNG, thus putting increased load on IGL’s existing CNG infrastructure. Also a 
very large number of CNG run private vehicles from adjoining NCR towns, as also all CNG buses 
of UP State Road Transport Corporation and Ha ryana Roadways originating from NCR towns, 
are being filled in Delhi due to absence of CNG fuelling facilities in NCR towns.  
 As regards development of CNG infrastructure in the cities of Gurgaon and Faridabad in 
Haryana, the State Government of Haryana did not give permission to IGL to operate. 
Subsequently, the Hon’ble Supreme Court gave interim direction in MC Mehta vs Union of India 
and other (13029/1985) on 04.04.2008 inter alia  that IGL supplies CNG in Gurgaon and 
Faridabad to two private parties, which would develop the CNG infrastructure in those cities. At 
present, IGL is supplying CNG to Gurgaon thro ugh cascades and only two daughter booster 
CNG stations have been started there.

 (d) To increase the number of CNG stations in Delhi, IGL has taken up the matter with

 16
• On October 20, 2008, the RBI reduced the repo rate to 8 per cent from the earlier

particularly on account of higher international crude petroleum prices; and the appreciation of 
the US dollar against major currencies since th e worsening of the global financial crisis

 †332. SHRI MANOHAR JOSHI: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to state:

†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

 37
 (b) whether it is also a fact that except in flight service department, the officers of Grade 
9A of all other departments have been promoted to the post of Assistant Manager;

of Assistant Manager; 
 (d) if so, the details thereof; and 
 (e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): 
(a) to (e) In erstwhile Indian Airlines Limited,  appointments to the post of Assistant Manager 
takes place through three channels - 30% of the available vacancies are filled through 
Promotion Quota from amongst Senior Superinten dents  of the cadre as per the laid down 
eligibility and selection process 30% of the av ailable vacancies are filled through selection 
Quota, which is open to employees of differ ent cadres based on eligibility and selection  
process, remaining 40% are filled through Dire ct  Recruitment Quota from open market  
where internal candidates are also allowed to  compete based on prescribed eligibility and 
selection process and upon being found suitable  preference in appointment goes to internal 
candidate. 
 Consequent to stagnation of senior employees and Promotion Quota vacancies being 
limited to 30% a tripartite settlement dated 9.2.2001 was signed with the representing union, 
i.e., Air Corporations Employees Union  to create a post of Officer in different cadres of  
non-technical ground staff category and it was decided that Senior Superintendents who  
used to qualify for consideration for appointm ent to the post of Assistant Manger under 
Promotion Quota after completion of 2 years of service would now be appointed as Officer to the 
extent of 15% of the standard force of Senior Superintendents. It was not assured to appoint 
them as Assistant Manager after 2 years. In fa ct they were to qualify for consideration  
for appointment to the post of Assistant Manager after completion of 2 years of service as an 
Officer and appointment was subject to availab ility of vacancies and the laid down selection 
process.  
 Subsequently, this dispensation was extended to  In flight Services Department also  though 
they has different service Regulations as flying crew and in their case the promotion quota was 
extended to 50% as against 30% for non-technical ground staff.  
 As a consequence of a recent unders tanding with the representing Union, i.e. Air 
Corporations Employees Union prior to merger of Air India Limited and Indian Airlines Limited, 
non-technical ground staff in the designation of Senior Superintendents who had completed 
more than 3 years of service as on 1st January 2 007 were appointed as Officer in their respective 
cadres and those who had completed 6 years of service were appointed to the post of Assistant 

 38
Manager in their respective cadres. This was done in order to create a near harmony in the levels 
between the non-technical ground staff of erstwh ile Air India and erstwhile Indian Airlines as 
against the demand of Union for total parity in career progression pattern since 1996 before 
merger was effected. While implementing this, su ch of the Senior Superintendents who were to 
be appointed directly to the post of Assistant Manager would have superseded the existing 
officers and to prevent th ese employees who were existing in the grade of Officers were first 
promoted to the post of Assistant Manager since majority of them in any case had rendered 
more than 6 years’ service as Senior Superintendents.

Outstanding Universal Value and be nominated as the property;

scope of the Sattras; 
 (iii) Undertake an appraisal of the overall ri ver basin in which Majuli lies and the potential 
impact of upstream development, deforestation and the building of dams, in order to 
ascertain whether managed retreat is the only  realistic approach to the flooding and 
erosion processes.

Protected monuments 
 351. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the Minister of CULTURE be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) permits use of protected monuments for 
the conduct of certain events on payment of charges; 
 (b)  if so, the details thereof including the na ture of events permitted and the charges fixed 
for it; 
 (c) whether the ASI had given such permission in past; and 
 (d)  if so, the details thereof during the last three years, year-wise and State-wise? 
 THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRIMATI AMBI KA SONI): (a) to (d) The Archaeological 
Survey of India permits usage of specific protec ted areas of some selected centrally protected 
monuments/sites in the country for holding cultural  events of high standard, preferably classical 
music, dance and drama on payment basis. The details of payment charged for their usage and 
the list of monuments/sites where such cultural events could be permitted under the guidelines 
issued by the Archaeological Survey of India is given in Statement-I  (See below). The details of 
holding cultural events at centrally protected mo numents during the last three years is given in 
Statement-II. 
Statement-I 
The Guidelines issued by the Archaeological Survey of India alongwith list of centrally protected 
monuments/sites where cultural events could be permitted 
1. As a matter of course, the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) will not like to permit the 
use of monuments and land attached to su ch monuments for holding functions/events. 
The circles may, however, permit such use only  as an exception if the DG, ASI/SA, circle 
is fully satisfied that the function/event is  unlikely to cause any damage, whatsoever, to 
the monument, its land and other built structures standing thereon. 
2. The circles would accord permission in only  those monuments, which are identified for 
holding cultural events. They will also delin eate the area/parts of the monument where 
such events can be held.  
3. The DG, ASI/SA, circle may refuse permission to hold functions in the identified 
monuments/sites in case ASI had undertaken recent renovation/beautification works and 
the holding of such event may interfere with the work / damage the renovations. 
4. If a monument is not listed for allowing the holding of cultural, the DG, ASI may grant such 
permissions after calling for a report from  the concerned SA. The DG, ASI however 
reserves the right to disallow any such request. His decision will be final.  

 49
5. Permission can be granted for holding cult ural events of a high standard, preferably 
classical. For this purpose, cultural even ts would mean classi cal music, dance and 
drama. In deciding whether an event is a cultural event or not, the decision of the DG, ASI 
would be final. 
6. No permission would be granted for any func tion / event where the admission is regulated 
by sale of tickets or by levy of admission charges. 
7. No permission would be granted for any ev ent which involves any commercial/ religious 
activity like sales, exhibition - cum - sales etc. 
8. Permission for holding functions would be granted only to Government departments and 
public bodies. No permission would be granted to private individuals, private bodies or 
other commercial organisations. In deciding whether the requests for holding a function is 
from a public body or not, the decision of the DG, ASI would be final. While considering 
the requests from public bodies, the DG, ASI / SA, circle would consider the previous 
history and activities of the organisation the purpose for which the event is being held and 
the nature and duration of the cultural event.  
9. Permission issued will be valid only for one day except in exceptional cases where for 
reasons to be recorded, such permissions may extend to more than one day. All 
temporary structures must be constructed and removed within the same day by 11 p.m. 
All function must conclude by 10 p.m. No music or loudspeaker etc. will be allowed 
thereafter. Any violation will lead to a police complaint by ASI officials.  
10. No construction activity of any type will be  permitted except for putting up a temporary 
rostrum or stage, which can be moved away. In putting up such temporary structures 
there will be no masonry activity. 
11. As the conduct of the even t within the monuments or its precincts is likely to cause 
damage to the built infrastructure and it s environs, the ASI would levy the following 
charges for usage:- 
 (i) For conducting an event in the land a ttached (outside) to a protected monument 
Rs.25000/- per day and where a part of the built monuments (inside) is also likely 
to be used along with the land Rs. 50000/- per day would be charged. (in select 
monuments in Delhi). 
 (ii) In other circles for conducting cultural event, Rs.10000/-  would be charged per 
day (for one day only) for using the ar ea attached (outside) to a protected 
monument and where a part of the protected  monuments is also likely to be used, 
Rs.25000/- per day would be charged. 
 D.G., ASI may decide if other differential needed.  

 50
 In addition to the above, ASI would also  demand a refundable security deposit of 
Rs.50000/- per day in all monuments in Delhi. In  other circles, this refundable security 
deposit would be Rs.30,000/-. This security deposit would be refunded within a week 
after the function after deducting expenditure, if any that the ASI has incurred in clearing 
the area of litter/garbage etc. or in repairing damages, if any. 
 The ASI would be free to impose appropriate conditions on various aspects like parking, 
maximum number of visitors, noise and luminous  levels etc. to ensure that the monument 
and its environs are protected  and preserved and the conduct of the event would not 
cause any damage to the monument (physically) or its cultural integrity. 
 A list of monuments where cultural events could be permitted is given at Statement  
(See below). This list is not exhaustive and the ASI may amend this list as and when 
required. 
 The above guidelines have come into force with effect from on 14th January, 2005.

Financial crisis in the USA 
 365. SHRI D. RAJA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
 (a)  whether Government’s attention has been drawn to the recent financial crisis in United 
States of America (USA); 
 (b)  if so, the details thereof; and 
 (c)  what is its impact on the Indian economy? 

 74
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINI STRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN KUMAR 
BANSAL): (a) to (c) The global financial crisis which surfaced in August 2007 had its origin in 
the meltdown of the US housing market and consequent sub-prime mortgage loan 
delinquencies and rising home foreclosures. This in turn led to a steep fall in the prices of 
mortgage-backed securities, whose value is de rived from mortgage payments. The financial 
institutions-investment banks, structured investment vehicles, hedge funds, etc. - with too little 
capital were unable to deal with the resultan t losses and write-downs. Further, as these 
institutions did not have recourse to central bank facilities, they were also unable to cope with 
the liquidity crunch that followed, thereby amp lifying the crisis. The tu rmoil in international 
financial markets intensified in  August-September, 2008 with the failure of major international 
financial institutions. 
 Indian banks have very limited exposure to the US mortgage market, directly or through 
derivatives, and to the failed and stressed internat ional financial institutions. The crisis in the 
international financial markets could impact th e Indian equity and fo reign exchange markets 
directly. The money, debt and credit markets coul d also be affected, albeit indirectly, raising 
costs of funds to Indian corporates. The macroe conomic impact of the global financial turmoil 
has been muted due to the overall strength of domestic demand and the predominantly 
domestic nature of financing of investment. The fundamentals of the Indian economy have been 
strong and continue of be strong. 
 The Government has been closely monitoring these developments in international 
financial markets and reviewing the emerging domestic financial market situation. There is a 
regular institutional mechanism in the form of a High Level Coordination Committee on 
Financial Markets (HLCCFM) with the Governor, RBI as Chairperson to oversee the regulatory 
and policy issues relating to Indian financial markets. The HLCCFM in its last meeting on 
October 1, 2008 reviewed the developments in the domestic financial markets and assessed 
the soundness of the systemic framework and the preparedness of all regulators to act in a 
coordinated and timely manner to deal with the emerging market situation in order to ensure 
smooth functioning of the markets.

 389. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to  
state: 
 (a)  whether the financial meltdown in the Un ited States of America (USA) would have any 
adverse impact on the investments which FIIs are making in our stock market; 
 (b)  if so, what is the projected financial bu rden and loss both to the stock market and the 
economy in particular; 
 (c)  how many financial companies would be pushed towards bankruptcy; 
 (d)  whether any steps have been mooted to address the issue; 
 (e)  if so, the details thereof; and 
 (f)  if not, the reasons therefor? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINI STRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN KUMAR 
BANSAL): (a) The global financial crisis which surfaced in August, 2007 had its origin in the 
meltdown of the US housing market. Pursuant to  this crisis and news about the bankruptcy  
of Lehman Brothers on September 15, 2008, Indian stock markets have witnessed a fall. As on 

 91
October 10, 2008, the Sensex had fallen by 49.6 per cent from its highest level on January 8, 
2008. The net equity investment by Flls during the period from August 17, 2007 to Dec. 31, 2007 
was USD 7.8 billion approximately. Since January, 2008, there has been a net disinvestment in 
equities to the tune of nearly $10.0 billion. 
 (b) and (c) The fundamentals of the Indian economy have been stro ng and continue to 
be strong. Our banking system is stable and sound. RBI has pointed out that Indian banks 
have very limited exposure to the US mortgage market (directly or through derivatives) or to 
the failed/stressed financial institutions; henc e the impact on their balance sheet will be 
marginal. 
 RBI has also informed that India’s real econ omy would be affected to a lesser degree than 
USA or Europe since our growth is largely domestically driven and our export markets not 
concentrated. Moreover, the current boom in the oil economies will be supportive of exports and 
inward remittances.  
 As regards the stock markets, it must be note d that the loss or gain arising from market 
movement is notional. In this context, it may also  be mentioned that only a very small portion of 
our total population, less than two per cent, has any sort of exposure to the stock market.  
 What we are witnessing today in the Indian markets is an indirect effect of the global 
financial situation. This is only a reflection of the uncertainty and anxiety in the global financial 
markets. However, there is no reason for any anxiety or uncertainty in India. 
 (d) to (f) Some of the steps taken by the Government, RBI and SEBI to balance the 
financial economy in the country are as follows:

on NR (E) Rupee deposits to LIBOR/Swap + 100 basis points

market. All the transactions by the RBI will be at prevailing market rates and as per 
market practice. 
 3. Allowing scheduled banks to avail additional liquidity support under the Liquidity 
Adjustment Facility (LAF) to the extent of upto one per cent of their Net Demand and 
Time Liabilities (NDTL) 
 4. Allowing banks to avail of  additional liquidity support exclusively for the purpose of 
meeting the liquidity requirements of natura l funds to the extent of upto 0.5 per cent 
of their NDTL 
 5. The Reserve Bank has decided to cond uct the second LAF on a daily basis with 
effect from September 17, 2008. 
 6. Reducing the Cash Reserve Ratio by 250 basis points from 9 per cent to 6.5 per cent 
of NDTL. 

 92
 7. Under the Agricultural Debt Waiver and Debt Relief Scheme, Government has agreed 
to provide to commercial banks, RRBs and co-operative credit institutions a sum of 
Rs.25,000 crore as the first installment. 
 8. It has been decided to increase the Fore ign Institutional Investors (FIIs) investment 
limit in corporate bonds from $3 billion to US$ 6 billion. 
 9. SEBI has decided that the position of  the securities lent by FIIs and their  
sub-accounts abroad shall be disseminated on a consolidated basis twice a week

financial institutions in India to ensure that  the orderly functioning of the market is not

 394. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
 (a)  whether it is a fact that recently th e Supreme Court took serious note of growing 
complaints of extra-legal methods used against loan defaulters and warned that banks must

10 points Reserve Bank of India (RBI) guidelines; and

recovery agents in the recent past, it is felt that the adverse publicity could result in serious 
reputational risk for the banking sector as a whole. Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has urged 
banks to follow prescribed guidelines while engaging recovery agents and has clarified that 
complaints received regarding abusive practices followed by a bank’s recovery agent would 
invite serious supervisory disapproval. RBI woul d consider imposing a temporary ban (or even 
a permanent ban in case of persistent abusive Practices), for engaging recovery agents, on

Court/Supreme Court or against its Directors/ Officers with regard to the abusive practices 
followed by their recovery agents. 

 95

RBI has advised the banks to ensure verificati on of antecedents of employees of recovery 
agencies engaged by them. Police verificat ion has been suggested as one of the  
pre-employment due diligence measures. RBI has also stipulated that all recovery agents should 
undergo a training-cum-certification programme offered by Indian Institute  of Banking and 
Finance (IIBF). 
 Further guidelines have also been issued by  RBI on Fair Practice for lenders. IBA has 
formulated a “Model Code for collection of dues and repossession of Security ”. The code of 
Bank’s commitments to customers has also been formulated by the Banking Codes and 
Standards Boards of India (BCSBI). All these gu idelines emphasise the fa ct that the collection 
policy of the Bank should be build on courtesy , fair treatment and persuasion and the bank

Global financial turmoil 
 403. DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJMA A. HEPTULLA: 
   SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: 
 Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
 (a)  whether a high-level meeting of financia l market regulators reviewed the preparedness 
of India to deal with challenges arising from ongoing global financial turmoil; 
 (b)  if so, the details of measures  discussed and taken in this regard; 
 (c)  whether as per statement by Prime Mini ster that India is not immune from what 
happens outside the world and what has been do ne to insulate the country to the maximum 
possible extent from the ill-effects of international financial market; and 
 (d)  if so, the details thereof? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINI STRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN KUMAR 
BANSAL): (a) The meeting of the High Level Coordination Committee of Financial Market 
(HLCCFM) was held on October 1, 2008 to discuss exclusively “the global financial turmoil with 
special reference to India’s preparedness”. 
 (b) to (d) In the above mentioned meeting and subsequently, it has been noted  
by the Government and the regulators that the fundamentals of the Indian economy have been 
strong and continue to be strong. Our bankin g system is stable and sound. What we are 
witnessing today in the Indian markets is an indirect effect of the global financial situation. This is 
only a reflection of the uncertainty and anxiety in the global financial markets. However, there is 
no reason for any anxiety or uncertainty in India. 

 109
 Some of the steps taken by the Governme nt, RBI and SEBI to balance the financial 
economy in the country are as follows: 
 1. Hike in interest rates on FCNR (B) de posits to LIBOR/Swap + 25 basis points and 
on NR (E) Rupee deposits to LIBOR/Swap + 100 basis points 
 2. Market intervention by RBI to augmen t supply in the domestic foreign exchange 
market. All the transactions by the RBI will be at prevailing market rates and as per 
market practice. 
 3. Allowing scheduled banks to avail additional liquidity support under the Liquidity 
Adjustment Facility (LAF) to the extent of up to one per cent of their Net Demand and 
Time Liabilities (NDTL) 
 4. Allowing banks to avail of  additional liquidity support exclusively for the purpose of 
meeting the liquidity requirements of mutual funds to the extent of up to 0.5 per cent 
of their NDTL 
 5. The Reserve Bank has decided to conduct the Second LAF on a daily basis with 
effect from September 17, 2008. 
 6. Reducing the Cash Reserve Ratio by 250 basis points from 9 per cent to 6.5 per cent 
of NDTL. 
 7. Under the Agricultural Debt Waiver and Debt Relief Scheme, Government has agreed 
to provide to commercial banks, RRBs and co-operative credit institutions a sum of 
Rs.25,000 crore as the first installment. 
 8. It has been decided to increase the Fore ign Institutional Investors (FIIs) investment 
limit in corporate bonds from $3 billion. 
 9. SEBI has decided that the position of the securities lent by FIIs and their sub-
accounts abroad shall be disseminated on a consolidated basis twice a week i.e. on 
Tuesday and Friday of every week. 
 10. SEBI has further informed that it has be en monitoring the activities of a few large 
financial institutions in India to ensure that  the orderly functioning of the market is not 
hampered. SEBI is also continuously reviewin g the situation in consultation with  the 
stock exchanges and the depositories. RB I - SEBI Technical Committee is also 
closely monitoring the developments in the global financial markets and its impact on 
the Indian markets.

 To check circulation of counterfeit currency, master circular have been issued by RBI 
advising banks that: 
 (i) Banks should ensure that they stock th eir ATMs with good quality genuine banknotes 
only. Disbursement of counterfeit notes through the ATMs would be treated as an 
attempt to circulate the counterfeit banknotes by the bank concerned.  
 (ii) Banks should establish at its Head Offi ce, a Forged (Counterfeit) Banknote Vigilance 
Cell to disseminate RBI instructions on co unterfeit banknotes to the branches and 
monitor the implementation of these instructions, to ensure that properly sorted and

safeguards both during the processing and transport of banknotes.  
 (iii) Banks should equip all the curren cy chests maintaining branches with  
note sorting machines to detect the counte rfeit notes. The banks may also consider 
setting up such machines at their branches and for public use at the counter.  
 (iv) Banks should undertake regular traini ng programmes for the staff on detection of 
counterfeit currency.  
 (v) In case counterfeit notes are found in  remittances from currency chests, entire 
amount equal to the value of counterfeit banknotes will be debited to the bank’s 
current account and penal interest will be levied on the amount of counterfeit 
banknotes from the date of previous remittance to RBI. 
 Further, RBI has been incorporating new Security features/new designs in the bank notes 
from time to time to stay ahead of counterfeiters.

 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS  
(SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL): (a) The under-recoveries of Public Sector Oil Marketing Companies 
(OMCs) on marketing of sensitive petroleum prod ucts were estimated at Rs.2.45 lakh crore in 
June, 2008 based on the approved principles of Import Parity pricing for PDS Kerosene and

 442. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA:

 Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
 (a)  the magnitude of salinity and water logging in irrigated commands, State-wise; 
 (b)  the reasons therefor; and 
 (c)  the corrective steps taken and their effectivity? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI JAI 
PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) Central Water Commission has recently carried out a study 
on “Assessment of water logging, saline and/ or al kaline soils in the commands of all major and 
medium irrigation commands in all the States of India and Union Territories, using satellite 
remote sensing”. The State-wise data is given in the Statement (See below). 
 (b) With the start of the pl anned irrigation development in the post independence era, 
farmers started using irrigation water in the ir rigated commands. In areas, where drainage was 
not adequate, this resulted in the rise of gr ound water table causing water logging and the 
seepage from unlined canals further contributed to  the Problem. The rise in ground water table 
brought the excessive harmful salts on the land surface causing salinity. 
 (c) Both preventive as well as ameliorati ve measures are being taken to check water 
logging and salinity. The preventive measures in clude lining of canals in vulnerable reaches,  
on-farm development works such as construction of lined field channels and drains, rotational 
supply (warabandi) of irrigation water to farmers, conjunctive us e of surface and ground water, 
propagation of improved methods of irrigation among farmers through training, adaptive trials 
and demonstrations. 
 Ameliorative measures include construction of surface and sub-surface drains, vertical 
drainage and bio-drainage for disposal of exce ss water and leaching of soil to flush out excess 
salts from root zone of crops. The above meas ures have proved effective in checking water 
logging and salinity.

Contaminated drinking water 
 †450. SHRI PRABHAT JHA: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
 (a)  whether it is a fact that out of the 123 countries of the World where large number of 
people are forced to drink contaminated water, India has been ranked at 121st position whereas 
our neighbouring countries i.e. Bangladesh and Sri Lanka are rank ed at 80th and 49th position 
respectively; 
 (b)  if so, the reaction of  Government’s thereto; and 
 (c)  the details of the steps being taken by Government to provide pure drinking water to all 
the people? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI JAI 
PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) Governme nt is not aware of any specific report 
stating that out of 123 countries of the World where a large number of people are forced to drink 
contaminated water, India has been raked at 121st positions whereas our neighbouring countries 
i.e. Bangladesh and Sri Lanka are ranked at 80th  and 49th positions respectively. However, 
several reports have indicated the ranking of vari ous countries on different issues from time to 
time. In the recently published Human Development Report 2007/2008 of United Nations 
Development Programme, out of a total of 177 countries, India has been shown at Sl. No. 128, 
where as Sri Lanka and Bangladesh are shown at Sl. No. 99 and 140 respectively in respect of 
“water, sanitation and nutritional status”. In an earlier United Nations World  Water Development 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

 145 
Report – “Water for People Water for Life ” published in 2003, a table titled “water quality 
indicator values in selected countries ” was included in which India was shown at Sl. No. 120. 
However, none of these reports have specific mention that “people are forced to drink 
contaminated water”. 
 (c) Ministry of Rural Development (Department of Drinking Water Supply) has taken a 
number of steps to enable the rural people to have access to safe drinking water in adequate 
quantity throughout the year on long-term basi s. Rural drinking water supply is the State 
subject. After 73rd Amendment in the Constitution  of India, rural drinking water as a subject 
has been put in the 11th Schedule to be transfer red to Panchayati Raj In stitutions. Government 
of India Supplements the efforts of the State Governments for providing safe drinking water in 
adequate quantity to the rural people of the country through the Centrally sponsored 
Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme. In 2005, the Government had launched a  
time-bound Bharat Nirman progr amme to provide safe drinking water to 55,067 uncovered 
habitations and 3.31 lakh slipped back habi tations along with addressing chemical 
contamination due to arsenic, fluoride, iron, salin ity and nitrate in 2.17 la kh rural habitations in 
the country during the period 2005-2009. In order to enable the community to check the water 
quality in all drinking water sources in the coun try, the Government had launched the National  
Rural Drinking Water Quality Monitoring and Surveillance Programme, wherein, 5 grassroot 
level workers are trained in each Gram Panchayat and given field test kits to test both 
chemical and biological contamination by themselves. Positively tested samples are then 
referred to the district water testing laboratory for confirmation and also to take necessary 
corrective action by the concerned water supply agency.

Action plan to meet devastation due to floods 
 458. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to 
state: 
 (a)  whether Government has decided any action plan to meet the devastation due to the 
floods in various parts of the country which normally hit during the monsoon season; 
 (b)  if so, how much money is earmarked to me et the eventualities in the States particularly 
to the flood affected districts of Andhra Pradesh for the present fiscal and also the details of the 
infrastructure proposed to be created for the purpose; and 
 (c)  if not, the reasons for not drawing on action plan? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI JAI 
PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) Flood Management being a State subject, the 
schemes for flood control are planned, funded an d executed by the State Governments, as per 
their own priorities, out of their State plans fu nds which are made available to them through 
Planning Commission. Expert Committees constituted by Government of India in the past to look 
into  the  problem of floods in the country observed that absolute immunity  from floods is not 

 154 
practically possible. However their impact can be  mitigated by way of suitable structural and 
non-structural measures. The recommendation s  o f  s u c h  E x p e r t  C o m m i t t e e s  h a v e  b e e n  
circulated to concerned Ministries/States for their implementation. 
 Government of India has also set up a National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) 
under Disaster Management Act, 2005 for manageme nt of natural calamities, including floods. 
The comprehensive guidelines on “Management of Floods ” issued by NDMA in January, 2008, 
inter alia , provides for preparation of flood manageme nt plans at national, State and district 
levels covering all aspect of disaster manageme nt cycle including the implementation schedule 
and monitoring system. These guidelines specify roles of central Ministries and States in disaster 
mitigation and relief. Ministry of Home Affairs pr ovides relief to the flood affected States under 
Calamity Relief Fund (CRF) and National Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF). 
 In addition, for providing ad ditional assistance to flood  affected States for flood 
management and erosion control works in crit ical reaches, the Government of India has 
approved a State sector scheme namely “Flood Management Programme ” with an estimated 
cost of Rs.8,000 crore for implementation during Eleventh plan. Under the scheme, no specific 
share of any State has been allocated. An Empowered Committee headed by Secretary 
(Expenditure) decides the eligible proposals of flood management works submitted by the State 
Governments for inclusion under Flood management Programme for central assistance.  
 (c) Does not arise.

 (a) whether a Bill, empowering the people to complain against corrupt Judges, would

Statement 
Empowering people to complain against corrupt Judges 
 (a) After examination of the Report of the Department Related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances and Law and Justice on the Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 
2006 and after careful consideration, the Govern ment have decided to withdraw the Judges 
(Inquiry) Bill, 2006 and introduce the Judges (Inquiry) Amendment Bill, 2008 in the current 
session of Parliament. 
 2. The salient features of the proposed Bill are the following: 
  (i) A National Judicial Council would be set up consisting of the Chief  
Justice of India, two seniormost Judges of the Supreme Court and Chief 
Justices of two High Courts, to be nominated by the Chief Justice of India. 
  (ii) The Council would be empowered to in vestigate and inquire into the allegations 
of misbehaviour or incapacity of a Judge of the Supreme Court or a Judge of the 
High Court, excluding the Chief Justice of India. 
  (iii) Any person can make a complaint in writing to the Council in respect of a Judge. 
  (iv) In case the Council finds the charge s of misbehaviour or incapacity to be 
proved, which do not warrant removal of a Judge, it may impose any or all of the 
following measures: 
   ( a )  I s s u i n g  a d v i s o r y ;  
   (b) Issuing warning; 
   (c) Withdrawal of judi cial work for some time; 
   (d) Request that the Judge may voluntarily retire; 
   (e) Censure or admoni tion, public or private. 
  (v) In case the Council concludes that charges have been proved and that these 
warrant the removal of a  Judge, it shall  advise the President accordingly. The 

 162
President shall place the findings of th e Council along with the accompanying 
material before the Parliament which would then act as per the prescribed 
procedure. 
  (vi) The Council shall issue a Code of Conduct containing Guidelines for conduct 
and behaviour of Judges.

 *25. SHRI VIJAY JAWAHARLAL DARDA: 
  SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
 Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether the Central Electricity Regulatory  Commission (CERC) has issued directions

 (b) if so, the details thereof;

 163
Electricity Grid Code and are ig noring the instructions of the Regional Load Despatch Centres 
(RLDC); and  
 (d) if so, the concrete steps Governme nt proposes to take in this regard? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY  OF POWER (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) 
and (b) The Indian Electricity Grid Code (IEG C) provides that the constituents should 
endeavour to restrict their net drawal from the grid within th eir respective drawal schedules 
whenever frequency is below 49.5 Hz. and carry  out requisite load shedding to curtail  
over-drawal when frequency falls below 49.0 Hz. The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission 
(CERC) has issued directions from time to time  to the Constituents/State Utilities, impressing 
upon them the need to maintain the safety an d stability of the Grid in accordance with the 
provisions of the Indian Electricity Grid Code (IEGC) notified by the Commission under Section 
178 of the Electricity Act, 2003. 
 (c) Yes, Sir. 
 (d) The Regional Load Despatch Centre being the designated apex body for monitoring of 
grid operations in the region, takes up the matt er with over-drawing constituents as and when 
required. In case of persistent default, notices ar e issued under Clause 1.5 of IEGC by Regional 
Load Despatch Centre and Member Secretary, Re gional Power Committee. The matter is also 
taken up by Central Transmission Utility, Centra l Electricity Authority and Ministry of Power 
whenever required. Secretary (Power), Govern ment of India had convened a meeting of 
constituent States/UTs of Northern, Western and Southern Regions on 12th September, 2008 
and inter alia directed them to curb over-drawal from the Grid. 
 Recently, vide order dated 22.09.2008 in Petition No.89/2008, after hearing the concerned 
parties, the CERC imposed penalty of One Lakh Rupees each on Transmission Corporation of 
Andhra Pradesh Limited, Karnat aka Power Transmission Limited,  Tamil Nadu Electricity Board 
and Kerala State Electricity Board for violation of Grid Code. 
 Subsequent to the issue of show cause notice  and imposition of penalty on the Southern 
Region Grid Constituents, improvement has been reported in Grid frequency of the Southern 
Region. 
 The Commission has vide its Order dated 16.10.2008 in suo-moto Petition No.  
115/2008, warned that penalty proceedings under section 142 of the Act may be resorted to by 
the Commission for each instance of violation of gr id discipline and that provision of section 149 
of the Act may be invoked for action against the person in-charge of and responsible for the 
affairs of the defaulting utility. The Commission ha s further directed the RLDCs to report within 3 
days block-wise over-drawls made by each State utility at grid frequency less than 49.0 Hz. 
RLDCs have also been directed to report within 3 days each case of non-compliance of their 
directions, to the Commission with all the necessary details such as nature of default, details of 
the directions, outcome of the direction, for action under section 29 of the Act, if found fit by the 
Commission.

Arbitrary fees by private educational institutions 
 †*31. SHRI PRABHAT JHA: Will the Minist er of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Government is aware that fees are charged arbitrarily from the students in the 
name of self-financed curricula by private educational institutions; 
 (b) whether Government has received an y complaint in respect of the above; 
 (c) whether Government is contemplating to implement in private colleges also the 
recommendations of the committee, constituted by  the UGC for effecting equal fee structure in 
universities and colleges of the country; and 
 (d) if so, the details thereof and by when the same would be implemented? 
 THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE D EVELOPMENT (SHRI ARJUN SINGH): (a) to 
(d) Yes Sir, while there are no specific complain ts received in the Ministry of Human Resource 
Development in this regard the Government is aw are that as private educational institutions do 
not generally receive financial assistance from public outlays, fees charged by them are relatively 
higher than those in the publicly funded institutions. However, All India Council for Technical 
Education (AICTE) has received five complaints in the recent past in respect of donation 
charged by private engineering/management inst itutions and the same are under investigation 
by the Council. 
 The Supreme Court in the matter of TMA Pai Foundation and Others vs. State of Karnataka 
[WP (Civil) No. 317 of 1995] has held that "in th e establishment of an educational institution, 
the object should not be to make a profit in as  much as education is essentially charitable in 
nature. There can, however, be a reasonable re venue surplus, which may be generated by the 
educational institution for the purpose of development of education and expansion of the 
institution". The Apex Court also held in its majority judgement in the same Writ Petition That "in 
as much as the occupation of education is, in a sense, regarded as charitable, the Government 
can provide regulations that will ensure excellence in education, while forbidding the charging of 
capitation fee and profiteering by the institution". 
 Accordingly, to regulate exorbitant fees which the private educational institutions may 
otherwise charge, the Government directed the University Grants Commission (UGC) to frame 
regulations for admissions and fee structure in private educational institutions in consultation with 
the stakeholders. The UGC constituted an Expert Committee in August, 2007 under the 
chairmanship of Prof. B.S. Sonde to formulate, inter alia, regulations with regard to admission 
and fee for self-financing private professi onal institutions, including 'deemed-to-be-
universities'. The Committee has submitted its report to the UGC and it is being examined by the 
Commission for making its recommendations to the Government. 
 Similarly, the AICTE is examining the aspect of  uniform guidelines for fee in AICTE approved 
technical institutions in the country. Accordin gly, it has constitute d a committee under the 
chairmanship of Justice Shri Ranganath Mishra, former Chief Justice of India.

reduction of curriculum load, em phasis on comprehension and application of knowledge, focus 
on continuous and comprehensive evaluation, emph asis on testing of competencies rather than 
rote memory, making examination more flexib le, provision of guidance and counseling in 
schools, and over all, to make learning child-centric. 
 Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) has taken the following steps to reduce fear 
of examination:

based assessment,

knowledge and understanding rather than rote memory,

to read question papers thoroughly,

though the total period of examination is 3 hours, 
 f. Shift from content based testing to problem solving and competency based testing,

also online,

declaration of the result of the main ex amination. Five chances are given in two

IGCC technology for power Generation 
 *36. SHRI MOINUL HASSAN: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether BHEL has entered into an agreement with the Andhra Pradesh Power 
Generation Corporation, to set up a 125. MW power, plants using the Integrated Gasification 
Combined Cycle (IGCC) technology; 
 (b) if so, whether IGCC technology is more th ermal efficient than conventional pulverized 
coal technology and is cost effective too; and 
 (c) if so, the comparative figures thereof? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY  OF POWER (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) 
Yes, Sir. 
 (b) and (c) Integrated Gasification Comb ined Cycle (IGCC) technology has been 
internationally tried mostly with petroleum fuels and low ash coals; It has not been proven in 
commercial level size plants with high ash, low quality Indian coals. The efficiency of IGCC 
process is dependent on the coal quality and al so other site conditio ns like ambient air and 
cooling water temperature and as such the efficien cy under Indian conditions is expected to be 
lower than what has been achieved internationally. 
 Studies were conducted by NTPC Ltd., for setting up of an IGCC demonstration plant in 
India. According to these studies, overall cost of  IGCC demonstration plant is  substantially 

 176
higher than the cost of smaller si ze conventional pulverized coal fired plant. Approximate cost of 
125 MW IGCC demonstration plant is about Rs. 8 crore per megawatt in comparison to around 
Rs.4.5 crore per megawatt for the pulverized coal fired plant. 
 As IGCC technology for Indian coals is yet to be developed for commercial level size plants 
comparative figures for efficiency will be known only after results are available from a suitably 
sized demonstration project. However, BHEL st udies indicate that corresponding to an 
efficiency of about 37% on high heating valu e (HHV) of a pulverized coal power plant of 
comparable 125 MW capacity, the efficiency of 125 MW IGCC plant is expected to be more than 
38% which may even go above 40% during commercial operational use.

Coaching for admission to IITs and Engineering Colleges 
 163. SHRI MOINUL HASSAN: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Government’s attention has been drawn to the fact that coaching for 
admission to the IITs and engineering colleges has acquired the status of a big industry in the 
country; and 
 (b) if so, what steps Government proposes to take in this matter? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI) : (a) and (b) With a view to curb the undue and undesirable 
burden on the school going children and mushrooming of the coaching Institutions and for giving 
due weightage to the marks obtained in qualifying board examination, the IIT-Joint Entrance 
Exam (JEE) has undergone major changes from 2006 onwards. Following reforms have been 
made in the pattern of IIT-JEE exam from 2006: 
 (i) JEE continued to be the sole criterion for ranking the students for admission in IITs, 
IT-BHU, ISM, Dhanbad and other participating institutes; 
 (ii) School results are factored into admiss ion process for the IITs. Only those students 
who secure a first-class or equivalent in the +2 examination are eligible for admission 
to the IITs; 
 (iii) For the students belonging to SC/ST, th ere is a relaxation of 5% of marks below the 
level of the marks prescribed in the respective examination; 
 (iv) JEE is a single objective type examin ation. The question paper can include short 
write-up on a topic in physics, chemistry or even mathematics followed by objective 
questions that are based on the write-up. This tests the comprehension ability as well 
as analytical ability of the student while retaining the objective character of the test. 
 (v) A student can write the JEE in the year in which he or she passes the 12th standard 
examination and/or in the following year; 
 (vi) Those who join any of  the IITs are not allowed to sit for the JEE again.

 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) As per the information received from the Government of

 (b) Whereas reports on cases of students committing suicide have appeared in

 (c) to (e) Although no specific study has been  conducted on the stress level of students. 
Government of India recognizes the need to ta ke measures to reduce the examination related 
stress among students. The National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) 
and Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) have taken several measures to reduce the 
examination related stress among students. National Curriculum Framework (NCF), 2005 
recommends measures like reduction of curric ulum load, emphasis on comprehension and 
application of knowledge, focus on continuous  and comprehensive evaluation, emphasis on 
testing of competencies rather than rote memory, making examination more flexible, provision of 
guidance and counselling in schools, and over all, to make learning child-centric. Central Board 
of Secondary Education has taken several steps including introduction of continuous and 
comprehensive evaluation, reconstruction of ex amination system, giving higher weightage to

declaration of results and provision of counselling services to students.

Promotion of higher education in tribal areas 
 192. SHRI JAI PRAKASH NARAYAN SINGH: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
 (a)  whether any policy has been formulated to promote higher education in tribal areas; 
and 
 (b)  if so, the details thereof and how ma ny students would be benefited from the  
same? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) and (b) The thrust of the policy underlying the XIth Plan 
for Higher Education is on increasing access to quality higher education while ensuring equity. A 
new Scheme for Reduction in Regional Imbalances, Social Gaps and Promotion of Inclusiveness 
in Higher Education has been introduced by the University Grants Commission in the XI Plan, 
which will serve the tribal areas as well. Central Universities have been established in all the 
States in the North-Eastern Region including in States with predominatel y tribal population. In 
addition, during the XI Plan a Central University will be established in each of those States where 
there is no Central University. 374 new college s are proposed to be established one in each 
district where the Gross Enrolment Ratio is lower than the national average. A scheme has also 
been drawn up to provide grants on a sharing basis to the universities and colleges which are not 
eligible for central assistance under the University Grants Commission Act, 1956 including those 
located in tribal areas. There are also scheme s for scholarships for Scheduled Tribe students 
and construction of girls' hostels in Colleges and Universities serving areas of low access to 
higher education. 
 In addition, the Indira Gandhi National Trib al University has been established, with its 
headquarters at Amarkantak in Madhya Pradesh, to provide avenues of higher education and 
research facilities primarily for the tribal populati on of the country. The University is empowered 
to open such number of  Regional Centres and Campuses in tribal areas as the University may 
deem fit.

Coaching institutions for IIT-JEE 
 204. SHRI S. ANBALAGAN: Will the Minist er of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Government is aware of the mushrooming of coaching institutions for IIT-
Joint Entrance Examination which charge exhorbitant fees from aspirants and the situation is that 
only who join costly institutions can make it to IITs; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof and the steps pr oposed to be taken by Government thereon; 
 (c) whether there is any proposal to scrap JEE and to have one (single) umbrella 
entrance test for all the Central Technology/ En gineering Educational Institutions through AIEEE 
which should be strictly based on 12th standard syllabus of the Central/State Boards; and 
 (d) if so, the details thereof an d if not, the reasons therefor? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) and (b) With  a view to curb the undue and undesirable 
burden on the school going children and mushrooming of the coaching Institutions and for giving 
due weightage to the marks obtained in qualifying board examination, the IIT-Joint Entrance 
Exam (JEE) has undergone major changes from 2006 onwards. Following reforms have been 
made in the pattern of IIT-JEE exam from 2006. 
 (i) JEE continued to be the sole criterion for ranking the students for admission in IITs, 
IT-BHU, ISM, Dhanbad and other participating institutes; 
 (ii) School results are factored into admiss ion process for the IITs. Only those students 
who secure a first-class or equivalent in the +2 examination are eligible for admission 
to the IITs; 
 (iii) For the students belonging to SC/ST, th ere is a relaxation of 5% of marks below the 
level of the Marks prescribed in the respective examination; 

 223
 (iv) JEE is a single objective type examin ation. The question paper can include short 
write-up on a topic in physics, chemistry or even mathematics followed by objective 
questions that are based on the write-up. This tests the comprehension ability as well 
as analytical ability of the student while retaining the objective character of the test. 
 (v) A student can write the JEE in the year in which he or she passes the 12th standard 
examination and/or in the following year; 
 (vi) Those who join any of  the IITs are not allowed to sit for the JEE again. 
 (c) and (d) There is no proposal to scrap JEE and have single umbrella entrance test for all 
the Central Technology/Engineering Educational Institutions through AIEEE. The JEE is 
conducted for admissions into IITs, Institute of Technology BHU, Varanasi and Indian School of 
Mines University, Dhanbad only, so as to maintain the high level of standards of these 
institutions. The Central Board of Secondar y Education (CBSE) conducts the All India 
Engineering Entrance Examination (AIEEE) for admissions to the under graduate programmes in 
Engineering, Architecture and Plan ning in the National Institutes  of Technology (NITs), Indian 
Institutes of Information Technology (IIITs), National Institutes of Foundry and Forge Technology 
(NIFFT), Ranchi, School of Planning and Architec ture (SPA), New Delhi and other Institutes of 
the Central Government.

 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINI STRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) to (c) On the occasion of the 400th Anniversary of the 
installation of Sri Guru Granth Sahib at the Golden Temple, the Prime Minister and announced that

Setting up of family courts 
 217. DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to 
state: 

 241 
 (a)  whether the Prime Minister has pointed out that many State Governments have failed 
to set up family courts, though it was their obligat ion to set up at least one family court in every 
district; 
 (b)  if so, whether it was aimed at adoption of a conciliatory approach in such cases, 
giving preference to mutual settlement over adjudication by the court; 
 (c)  if so, how many States have not set up these family courts so far; 
 (d)  what are the main reasons; 
 (e)  whether any directive has been issued by the Ministry to these States to set up family 
courts, to remove backlog in various courts; and 
 (f)  if so, the details thereof? 
 THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDW AJ): (a) Yes, Sir. The 
Hon’ble Prime Minister, during his address at the Conference of Chief Ministers and Chief 
Justices of High Courts held on 19th April 2008, mentioned that the Family Court Act, 1984 
mandates State Governments to establish Family Courts in urban areas with a population  of 
over one million. Many State Governments have not discharged their legal obligation in this 
regard.  
 (b) The Family Courts Act was enacted in 1984 for settlement of family disputes in a 
congenial atmosphere. The Act makes it obligatory on the part of the Family Court to endeavour, 
in the first instance to effect a reconciliation or a settlement between the parties to a family 
dispute. During this stage, the proceedings will be  informal and the rigid rules of procedure shall 
not apply. 
 (c) and (d) Twelve States/UTs have not set up  any family court so far. The Government of 
Arunachal Pradesh has informed that the State does not have a single town or city whose 
population exceeds one million and also that all th e family disputes are settled as per customary 
and personal law of the indigenous population of Arunachal Pradesh. Similarly the Government 
of Goa has informed that there appears to be no requirement for establishment of Family Court in 
the State. Also, the Government of J and K has in formed that since the Family Court Act is not 
applicable to the State, no family court has been established in the State.  
 (e) and (f) Chief Ministers/ Administrators of all the State Governments/ Union Territories 
have been requested to establish Family Courts in all Districts of the country.

 230. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to

 THE MINISTER OF LAW  AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): (a) to (d) The issue of 
Judicial Accountability was discussed at the Conference of Chief Justices held in 1990 and no the 
basis of the broad consensus em erging out of the deliberations , the Chief Justice of India

 250
  “The Chief Justice of the High Court ha s the competence to receive complaints 
against the conduct of the Judges of his court and when he receives any he would 
look into it for finding out if it deserves to  be closely looked into. Where he is satisfied 
that the matter requires to be examined, he shall have facts ascertained in such 
manner as he considers appropriate keeping the nature of allegations in view and if he 
is of the opinion that the matter is such that  it should be reported to the Chief Justice 
of India, he shall do so. 
  The Chief Justice of India shall act in a si milar manner in regard to complaints relating 
to conduct of Judges of the Supreme Co urt and in regard to conduct of Chief 
Justices of the High Courts. On the basis of the facts ascertained, the Chief Justice 
of the High Court or the Supreme Court,  as the case may be, shall take such 
appropriate action as may be considered  proper, keeping the interests of the 
Judiciary as the paramount consideration.” 
 The complaints received against the Judges of  the Supreme Court and the High Courts are,

incorporating a number of recommendations made by the Standing Committee.

implementing the Remote Village Electrification  Programme for providing basic facilities of 
lighting/electricity in all the eligible remote, unelectrified census villages and hamlets through

villages and hamlets. A target of covering 1500 remote villages and hamlets has been set for the 
year 2008-09.

Electrification Programme depends upon identification of such villages by the states and 
submission of proposals by them as per the Pr ogramme provisions. Financial support to such 
proposals is considered in the Ministry on case-to-case basis and subject to availability of funds.

Setting up of mega power plants 
 258. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
 (a)  whether it is a fact that foreign compan ies have been invited to build, own and operate 
mega power plants in the country; 
 (b)  if so, the rationale behi nd permitting the foreign Compan ies to invest/participate in 
this strategic sector; and 
 (c)  what safeguards are built into the agre ements to prevent any company from resorting 
to arm twisting practices in the grid management of the country? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) 
and (b) The policy to encourage greater private s ector participation in the electricity sector 
was announced in 1991 with the objective of bringing in additionality of resources for the 
capacity addition programme which subsequently included Mega Power Projects. Since then 
privately owned enterprises, including foreign companies have been allowed in the electricity 
sector.  
 After the enactment of the Electricity Act, 2003,  concurrence of Central Electricity Authority 
(CEA) is not required for setting up of thermal power plants including those in the private sector. 
In case of hydel projects, concurrence of CEA is  required under Section 8(1) of the Electricity 
Act for setting up of a hydro power generation st ation estimated to involve a capital expenditure 
exceeding the sum notified by the Central Government.  
 Further, under the existing policy of the Government, Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is 
permitted in the power sector on the automa tic route wherein no prior approval of the 
Government is required except when the foreig n investor has an existing collaboration/joint 
venture in the same sector.  
 (c) Grid management and operation is the responsibility of the Load Dispatch Centre 
which is to be operated by a Government Company or organization as per sections 26, 27 and 31 
of the Electricity Act, 2003. Section 28 of the Ac t provides that the Regional Load Dispatch 
Centre (RLDC) shall be the apex body to ensure integrated operation of the power system in the 

 274
concerned region. The RLDC discharges its functions in accordance, inter alia, with the Grid 
Code specified by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC). CERC has notified the 
Grid Code which provides, inter alia, for t echnical rules for operation, maintenance, 
development and planning of economic and relia ble regional grid. Ev ery grid constituent 
including the generating company owning and op erating the mega power plant is required to 
comply with the grid code specified by the Commission. The Act has adequate provisions to deal 
with violation of the rules and regulations made thereunder.

Functioning of APDRP 
 260. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Mini ster of POWER be pleased to state: 
 (a)  whether the Accelerated Power Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) has 
targeted to bring down aggregate technical and commercial losses of power utilities to fifteen per 
cent, within five years; 
 (b)  whether Government has provided the su pport for State power utilities for the projects 
under APDRP and if so, the details thereof; and 
 (c)  whether Government intends to make this support to States conditional, as a 
performance based incentive, rather than an assured one? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY  OF POWER (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) 
Government had launched Accelerated Power Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) 
in the year 2002-03 with the objective of encouraging reforms and of reduction in Aggregate 
Technical and Commercial (AT and C) loss, improving quality of supply of power and improving 
consumer satisfaction. The target was to reduce AT and C losses to 15% in five years in urban 
and high density consumption areas, to begin with.  
 (b) Government of India had sanctioned projects amounting to Rs.17033.58 crore under 
the investment component for strengthening and upgradation of sub-transmission and 
distribution systems of the States. The States have so far utilized Rs.11279.50 crores. An amount 
of Rs. 2879.73 crore has also been released to nine  states for achieving reduction in cash losses 
under the incentive component of the programme.  
 (c) The Government have approved the continuation of  Accelerated Power Development 
and Reforms Programme (APDRP) during the Eleventh   Five Year Plan with revised terms and 

 276
conditions as a Central Sector Scheme. The focus of the programme is on actual, demonstrable 
performance in terms of loss reduction. Establishment of reliable and automated systems for 
sustained collection of accurate base line data, and the adoption of Information Technology in 
the areas of energy accounting are the necessary pre-conditions before sanctioning any 
projects for strengthening and up-gradation of  Sub-transmission and distribution networks. 
Projects under the scheme are to be taken up in Two Parts. Part-A is to include the projects 
for establishment of baseline data and IT applications for energy accounting / auditing and IT 
based consumer service centers. Part-B includes  regular distribution strengthening projects. 
Initially funds for projects under both parts sh all be provided through loan. Government of 
India will provide the permissible grant money as  and when it becomes payable. The entire 
amount of loan for Part-A Projects is to be converted into grant once the establishment of the 
required Baseline data system is achieved and verified by an independent agency appointed  
by the Ministry of Power. Up to 50% (90% for special category states) of loan for Part-B 
projects is to be converted into grant on achieving the 15% AT and C loss in the project  
area. The Utilities are also to achieve the following target of AT and C loss reduction at utility 
level:  
 • Utilities having AT and C loss above 30%: Reduction by 3% per year 
 • Utilities having AT and C loss below 30%: Reduction by 1.5% per year
